decisions.source: docs/proposals/03_AUDIO_VIDEO.md §16 row 1 (line 812); rulings text §11 lines 623-627; §13 S0 (line 680). Amended by 03b §0b.6 ('§16 Row 1: R-OPT fresh group and freeze shift stamp' superseded) and 03b §13 'S0 Rulings adds'
decisions.question: Adopt the S0 rulings: M1 one Windows kind; the transport-id layout (MEDIA_ID_BASE 1<<24, MEDIA_BLOCK 1<<20, MODALITY_INDEX aud 0 / vid 1 / img 2 reserved); R-CKPT absent-field rule; R-SIG bytes->typed alphabet widening; R-OPT fresh optimizer group (and, in 03, the freeze shift stamp)?
decisions.options: Adopt all as written; adopt in part; split clock kinds instead of one Windows kind (rejected in 03 §14). 03b replaces the 'freeze shift stamp' clause (the codec group never retires except in the frozen control arm; stamps come from acts) and adds R-LIVE, R-RESUME-AT-ACT, R-RATE, the R-OPT extension (OPT.retire_group), Q-TOK-15, Q-MEM-13, Q-RUN-16, Q-LM-13, Q-SIG-3, Q-OPT-10, Q-OPT-11, Q-MEM-14, Q-DOM-4, Q-CKPT-5.
decisions.current_recommendation: Adopt all as written (03). The 'freeze shift stamp' half of R-OPT is superseded by 03b; the rest stands (03b §16: 'Rows 1, 3-10 and 12 stand').

Split kinds rejected: 'multiplies every cadence lever for no type-safety gain' (03 §14). S0b already built Q-RUN-16, Q-MEM-13 and Q-OPT-10 (commits 54378b8, c8d8e33, c5768be; docs/04_CONTRACT.md headings dated 2026-09-26). No measurement decides this: it is a contract ruling.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03_AUDIO_VIDEO.md §16 row 2 (line 813); replaced by docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 2 (line 1375) and §0b.6
decisions.question: Frame rate: 25 or 50 Hz?
decisions.options: Build both behind one lever with default 25 Hz (03); 50 Hz; the rate measured per run (03b)
decisions.current_recommendation: 03's 'default 25 Hz' is SUPERSEDED by 03b row 2: AUD_RATE_MODE='measured' per run, with 'fixed' stride 2 as the control.
decisions.evidence: The 03 rationale was a 25 Hz LM advantage measured on a 109-code SEANet codec, not the 559-code spectral codec. Spectral 25 Hz probe exact on reconstructions 44.4% vs 50 Hz 40.3% (03 §6.1 table). Owner, 2026-09-25: 'I am also reconsidering the hz'.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03_AUDIO_VIDEO.md §16 row 3 (line 814); §5 conditional move #9; §13 S8 arm 1; 03b §16 preamble (row stands); 03b §13 S8 arm 2
decisions.question: Promote the continuous insert for understanding (LM.encode(..., media=)) from S8 to S5, as an arm?
decisions.options: Promote to S5 as an off arm; leave it at S8; make it the default understanding path
decisions.current_recommendation: Yes, as an arm, default off. The default waits for grounding-per-FLOP.
decisions.evidence: Discrete understanding reached 45-55% of a dedicated code classifier; the continuous insert reached 0.94-0.98 (Route 2: 0.978 notes vs 0.485). Building it early costs one frozen-signature move. results/multimodal_design_2026-09-25/prototypes/design-world/. Decider: S8 arm (a) judged on grounding per FLOP (owed).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03_AUDIO_VIDEO.md §16 row 4 (line 815); §8 measured baselines table; Appendix B S4/S5 (d)
decisions.question: Composition is near zero in every route: is it a scale problem or a data-variety problem?
decisions.options: GPU width x data sweep on the combination split (LM width 128/256/512 x media seconds per epoch 600/3,000/15,000); more generator variety; architectural arms (continuous insert, WORLD rollout)
decisions.current_recommendation: Run the GPU width x data sweep on the combination split (Appendix B S4/S5 d).
decisions.evidence: Route 3 held-out combinations: understanding exact 0%, generation 0-8% (03 §8 table). Route 2's WORLD rollout gets the first note wrong in every held-out combination (0.0) (03 §14). Owed: the owner's GPU sweep at S4/S5. Held-out combinations are the most direct generalization reading in the design.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03_AUDIO_VIDEO.md §16 row 5 (line 816); 03b 'Contract accounting — deltas', Wires row
decisions.question: Wire budget with VID: stay inside 25 wires, or make a multi-source ruling?
decisions.options: Stay inside 25 (audio stages 21, VID 23, leaving 2); a multi-source ruling; free 2 wires by deleting the CAP reporting rows (Q-CLOCK-1 option b)

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03_AUDIO_VIDEO.md §16 row 6 (line 817)
decisions.question: Where does the synthetic generator code live?
decisions.options: Private functions in data/api.py; a helper module, which needs its own ruling
decisions.current_recommendation: Private functions in data/api.py.
decisions.evidence: The package rule is api.py + levers.py. A helper module needs its own ruling and buys nothing measurable. No measurement applies.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03_AUDIO_VIDEO.md §16 row 7 (line 818); §8
decisions.question: Is a perceptual metric trained from scratch allowed for real data later?
decisions.options: Evaluation only; also as a training loss; not at all (pretrained metrics are excluded either way)
decisions.current_recommendation: Allowed for evaluation only, never as a training loss.
decisions.evidence: This keeps 'learned from scratch' and keeps pretrained weights out. The learned probe is fragile: 2.3% on reconstructions before augmentation (03 §8). Analytic recovery is the primary reading.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03_AUDIO_VIDEO.md §16 row 8 (line 819); §5 conditional move #8; §9 MEM bullet; S8 arm 8
decisions.question: MEM over media: a default after the S8 arm, or text-only?
decisions.options: Text-only first with MEM-over-media as an S8 arm (MEM.open_store(media_spans=), MEM_MEDIA); MEM over media by default
decisions.current_recommendation: Text-only first; MEM over media is an S8 arm.
decisions.evidence: MEM's keys are text-shaped today. The per-source floor counts text sources only, so media never shrinks text's protected memory (03 §9). Decider: the S8 (g) arm (owed).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03_AUDIO_VIDEO.md §16 row 9 (line 820); §9 table; Appendix B S4/S5 (e)
decisions.question: How is text protected when media arrives: rehearsal (DATA_TEXT_SHARE), an lr-shield, or a freeze?
decisions.options: Rehearsal at DATA_TEXT_SHARE 0.1 / 0.3 / 0.5; an lr-shield of text rows and experts (re-warm at the boundary); zero-born gates; upcycling; generative self-replay; freezing (rejected)
decisions.current_recommendation: Rehearsal default 0.3; the lr-shield built as an arm; freezing rejected (a downgrade: text stops improving).
decisions.evidence: 03 §9: Route 1 pure-add 2.966->3.196 bits/token (+7.8%), WORLD text MSE 1.02->3.21; 30% replay 2.966->2.906 (text still improving); Route 3 pure-add (masked) 1.936->7.846 bits/byte; 25% replay 1.936->1.931. Rehearsal was measured sufficient at 25-30%. Decider: App B S4/S5 (e), pure-add vs rehearsed at 0.1/0.3/0.5 vs lr-shield (owed). The lr-shield relies on OPT_LR_SHIFT_WARM, which ships 0.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03_AUDIO_VIDEO.md §16 row 10 (line 821); §6.1; amended by 03b §16 row 13
decisions.question: Is envelope-level audio (spectral codec + Griffin-Lim) acceptable for the first cut?
decisions.options: Yes, with the 'wave' codec as an arm (S3 a); require waveform-level quality now; a learned vocoder (03b)
decisions.current_recommendation: Yes, with the 'wave' codec built as an arm. 03b adds that Griffin-Lim is not 'absolutely necessary', so a learned-vocoder arm is built (S8).
decisions.evidence: Synthetic families are exactly recoverable at envelope level. SEANet wave at 50 Hz: 2.8% probe (chance), near silent; wave 25 Hz: mel 1.03 (03 §6.1 table). Timbre is every codec's weak attribute (0.60).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03_AUDIO_VIDEO.md §16 row 11 (line 822); replaced by 03b §16 row 21 (line 1384)
decisions.question: How is the codec retrained on real data?
decisions.options: Versioned codec handover: a new id block with nearest-row init (03); in-place live adaptation (03b)
decisions.current_recommendation: SUPERSEDED by 03b row 21: the live codec adapts in place, and the handover is kept only for an architecture or lattice change.
decisions.evidence: 03's premise ('frozen ids must never change meaning inside a run') is removed by the live codec.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03_AUDIO_VIDEO.md §16 row 12 (line 823); §0 R11; amended by 03b §0b.6 (R11) and 0b.1 item 16
decisions.question: Who owns the per-modality running baselines that FAB competence and DOM.note_competence receive?
decisions.options: FAB owns them (state_dict key, restore row, geometry note) and DOM gets a copy as an argument; DOM owns them; the root holds them
decisions.current_recommendation: FAB. 03b amends R11: the root first converts each value to a segmentation-invariant unit (bits per build-time token for text, bits per clip-second for media), and the running baseline then normalises it.
decisions.evidence: FAB is the heavier consumer. There is no measurement: this is an ownership ruling.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 2 (line 1375); 0b.1 item 3; §6.3; 0b.3
decisions.question: How is the media frame rate chosen?
decisions.options: 'measured' per run at readiness (the coarsest of 50/25/12.5 Hz whose recover-exact is within AUD_RATE_TOL 0.05 of the finest); 'fixed' stride 2 (the control); per-segment arms 'alloc', 'bpe', 'router', 'measured_arrival'; 04's 'progress' arm
decisions.current_recommendation: 'measured' per run at readiness. 'fixed' stride 2 is the control, and 'alloc', 'bpe', 'router' and 'measured_arrival' are arms. S5 decides per-segment adaptivity.
decisions.evidence: On LM bits/s a fixed stride beat or tied every per-segment rate at toy scale (D3; D1 at 3 seeds; D2's router on mel at 2 seeds). Bits/s depends on the alphabet across rate arms, and the codec-invariant readings tie within noise. 1 s clips may fake a low-rate cliff. Forced 12.5 Hz cost +11.9/+11.6% tones codec mel against forced 25 Hz (nested codec, n = 36/32). The 'measured' rule itself was never prototyped. results/live_codec_design_2026-09-25/prototypes/{d1,d2,d3}. Decider: S5 rate sweep on 2-4 s clips (owed).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 13 (line 1376); 0b.3
decisions.question: Is a fixed non-learned transform 'absolutely necessary' (the analysis grid, the FSQ lattice, Griffin-Lim)?
decisions.options: Keep the grid and lattice as fixed like bytes, with learned alternatives as arms ('wave' front end; versioned-block handover); keep Griffin-Lim fixed; replace Griffin-Lim with a learned vocoder
decisions.current_recommendation: Grid (DATA_AUD_SR 8000, n_fft 512, hop 160 = 50 frames/s) and lattice (AUD_LEVELS 8,5,5,5): yes, like bytes, with learned alternatives as arms. Griffin-Lim: no; build the learned-vocoder arm.
decisions.evidence: Neither the grid nor the lattice has parameters, and each gives an id its unit or address. Griffin-Lim is a fixed stage where a learned one exists, and it may contribute to the timbre loss. Decider for the vocoder: S8/GPU arm judged on recover exact of decoded audio (owed).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 14 (line 1377); 0b.1 items 1, 6, 8; 0b.2 rows 1-2
decisions.question: What is the codec's default plasticity (how live the codec is)?
decisions.options: D1's measured regime; the 1/4 cadence; high plasticity; AUD_REWARM > 0; jit_ema; the frozen codec (control arm only)
decisions.current_recommendation: D1's measured regime: 1/32 cadence, floor 5e-5, D1's betas (0.8, 0.99), weight decay 0.01 and clip 1.0, anchor 10 to a snapshot refreshed at every act (at least every 2000 windows, 4000 under a guard hold), rehearsal 0.5. Re-warm off. AUD owns the codec schedule (Q-OPT-11). An S3 replica with its own frozen control confirms it, and S5 (ii) decides the cadence.
decisions.evidence: Live vs frozen at 4 paired LM seeds: bits/s (codec-dependent) lower in 24/24. LM-side codec-invariant readings: no consistent cost or gain (caption bits/byte worse 11/16, -8.7% to +7.9%; understanding worse 5/8; generation exact worse 12/32, better 18, tied 2). Codec ceiling: consistent cost (recover exact lower in 7 of 8 plus 1 tie). All on ONE codec init at 25 Hz with 4000 pre-train steps. The 1/4 cadence leaned better at 2 seeds (caption 3/4, understanding 2/2, recover exact 3/4), unreproduced, at about 2x CPU. High plasticity: -0.1% to +8.1% bits/s vs frozen (7/8 worse). results/live_codec_design_2026-09-25/prototypes/d1, rev/audit_d1.{py,txt}. Decider: S3 replica and S5 (ii) (owed).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 15 (line 1378); 0b.4; docs/04_CONTRACT.md Q-RUN-8 ruling (line 4219)
decisions.question: Adopt S0b, which changes every default run past window 3000?
decisions.options: Adopt, and ship TOK_RETOK_EVERY by the non-inferiority rule; keep the text segmentation frozen within an epoch
decisions.current_recommendation: Adopt it. Ship TOK_RETOK_EVERY by the non-inferiority rule (§13).
decisions.evidence: The owner, 2026-09-26: 'Stream rebuilding sounds important. I think it's a good way for the llm to learn'. Built in 54378b8, c8d8e33 and c5768be; Q-RUN-8 RESOLVED 2026-09-26. Without it about 600 minted rows per 20k-window run are stranded (0b.4, arithmetic). tests/test_continuation.py: 18 checks pass (c5768be).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 16 (line 1379); §13 S0b OPT row; docs/04_CONTRACT.md Q-OPT-10 (line 4936)
decisions.question: Is the OPT LR horizon revised after an act changes the epoch length?
decisions.options: OPT.revise_horizon, LR-continuous, on by default (OPT_HORIZON_REVISE True); keep the build-time horizon and print the residual (Q-OPT-5 (a))
decisions.current_recommendation: OPT.revise_horizon(opt, st, *, run_windows), default on, LR-continuous, and inert (ABSENT with its reason) when cycles_fitted > 1, under Q-OPT-10.
decisions.evidence: Without it Q-OPT-5's under-anneal occurs inside every run. The old per-epoch re-projection gave E8 p=0.760, E18 p=0.730 and H17. Known answer 17 (lr(now) kept to 1e-12, ends at the floor) is driven by tests/test_continuation.py S2. TREE GAP: no OPT_HORIZON_REVISE lever exists in src/opt/levers.py, and src/spine/loop.py:1233 calls opt_api.revise_horizon unconditionally, so there is no off arm.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 17 (line 1380); 0b.1 (coordinate rows); 0b.2 row 11; §13 S5 (iv)
decisions.question: Should coordinate rows be the default even though they raise cross-area interference?
decisions.options: LM_MEDIA_ROWS / SIG_MEDIA_ROWS 'coord' with DATA_MEDIA_REHEARSE 1/3; 'table'; DATA_MEDIA_REHEARSE 0
decisions.current_recommendation: Yes, 'coord' with DATA_MEDIA_REHEARSE 1/3. 'table' is a live S5 arm, plus the longer / larger-data check (S5 iv); 'table' returns to the default if the gain disappears while the interference stays.
decisions.evidence: A sample-efficiency gain at 4/4 seeds in both harnesses: -9.9% to -16.7% bits/s in D1 (one codec init, smaller at new seeds) and -11.3% to -15.3% in D3. It may shrink at scale while the interference stays, and it is not drift tolerance. 0b.2 row 11: interference measured as the rise of area A's bits/s after training on B, with no LM media rehearsal. Decider: S5 (iv) at 20k windows with 10x the prototypes' media LM steps (owed).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 18 (line 1381); 0b.1 item 8
decisions.question: A live codec improves mel and lowers timbre recovery: what is the codec's acceptance metric, and what guards it?
decisions.options: Recover exact as the acceptance metric with a per-family calibrated ceiling guard ('hold'); 'count' only; the 'multires' loss arm; re-warm
decisions.current_recommendation: Recover exact is the acceptance metric. The guard, calibrated per family above the measured spread, holds the snapshot. The 'multires' loss arm is built before re-warm can default on.
decisions.evidence: Timbre falls in D3 at high plasticity, not step-matched (tones 4/4, melody 3/4 plus a tie), and by less at D3's low plasticity (tones 2/2). Exact match falls in D1 (one codec init) and is mixed in D3. This is an objective misalignment, not a codec defect.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 19 (line 1382); 0b.1 item 18; 03 §14
decisions.question: Should the LM or WORLD shape the codec?
decisions.options: None (default); 'rep' and 'input' bounded couplings (AUD_LM_GRAD) as arms; full joint training (rejected)
decisions.current_recommendation: None by default. 'rep' and 'input' are arms.
decisions.evidence: Likelihood flowing into the codec collapses or concentrates the latent (REPA-E, STE collapse, AQM, cited in 03 §14). Bounded terms are unmeasured here. Decider: S8 'rep' arm (owed).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 20 (line 1383)
decisions.question: Media geometry: inline or separate windows?
decisions.options: 'inline' (DATA_MEDIA_GEOMETRY); 'windows'
decisions.current_recommendation: 'inline' by default; 'windows' is an arm (S8).
decisions.evidence: Inline supports interleaved documents and needs no act at a per-run stride. Unmeasured head to head.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 21 (line 1384), replacing 03 row 11
decisions.question: How is the codec retrained on real data?
decisions.options: In-place live adaptation; a re-warm at the area's arrival; a versioned block handover
decisions.current_recommendation: The live codec adapts in place. A re-warm at the area's arrival waits until S3 clears it. The versioned handover is only for an architecture or lattice change.
decisions.evidence: Media code meaning is no longer frozen within a run, and nothing persists codes. No real-audio measurement exists.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 22 (line 1385); 0b.1 item 14; docs/04_CONTRACT.md Q-RUN-16 (line 4894)
decisions.question: How does a run resume when the vocabulary or codec changed between acts?
decisions.options: (b) resume from the last act's recorded state (view, replay record, run-global rev, clock restore); (a) and (c), recorded as rejected
decisions.current_recommendation: Option (b).
decisions.evidence: Built in c8d8e33 (Q-RUN-16 RESOLVED 2026-09-26). tests/test_continuation.py reproduces the uninterrupted run's losses exactly in 4 cases (no act; a save between a mint and the next act; a save after an act; TOK_DROPOUT 0.1). It replaces Q-RUN-10's replay and closes Q-TOK-13's mint-burst item.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 23 (line 1386); 0b.1 item 5 (D-5)
decisions.question: Media codes: a snapshot taken at each act, or a just-in-time EMA?
decisions.options: AUD_CODES 'snapshot' (default); 'jit_ema' (with AUD_EMA_HALF_LIFE, AUD_SHIFT_FLIPS)
decisions.current_recommendation: Snapshot by default; 'jit_ema' is an arm.
decisions.evidence: The snapshot is the measured regime, gives an exact resume and one drift event per act. EMA's measured value is flip rate, not LM bits. Decider: S5 plasticity matrix (owed).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 24 (line 1387); 0b.1 item 4 (D-2)
decisions.question: Codec architecture: 'spec' or 'nested'?
decisions.options: 'spec' (per-stride candidates); 'nested' multi-rate; 'wave'; 'dmel'
decisions.current_recommendation: 'spec'. S3 decides with the per-attribute criterion and its non-inferiority margin.
decisions.evidence: 'nested' was lower on melody timbre at 3/3 seeds (one of the three beyond noise at n = 64) while winning tones mel. Decider: S3 at 2 seeds with AUD_PROBE_N 400 (owed).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 25 (line 1388)
decisions.question: Does the 'measured' rate rule need a mel term, or a larger probe?
decisions.options: No mel term with AUD_PROBE_N 400; add a mel term; raise n
decisions.current_recommendation: No mel term by default, and AUD_PROBE_N 400, read as a paired difference with its SE and the false-'out' estimate reported. Add a mel term if 'measured' picks a stride that loses on the primaries; raise n if the paired SE exceeds AUD_RATE_TOL / 2.
decisions.evidence: On the toy nested-codec readings, exact match alone would have picked 12.5 Hz where tones mel was +12%. The rule is unprototyped, and noise biases it toward stride 1. Decider: S5 checks 'measured' against every fixed stride (owed).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 26 (line 1389); 0b.1 item 16; 0b.4 per-token levels row; §13 S0b Levels row; S5 (iii)
decisions.question: How does the routing stack (SIG, DOM, FAB, MEM, CAP) cope with a moving tokenizer and codec?
decisions.options: Shift stamps at acts ('refresh' default; AUD_SHIFT_STAMP 'flips' / 'always'); re-keys; per-byte levels; MEM rescaled surprise; no stamps
decisions.current_recommendation: Coordinate signatures. Shift stamps to FAB and OPT (CAP from P4) at acts that move the text view, and at refreshing acts once media is consumed. DOM.on_retokenize whenever the view moved; the composed DOM.rekey at refresh acts at SIG_MODE=learned (Q-DOM-4). Bits per build-time token for DOM (and CAP from P4); MEM's rescaled surprise. S5 (iii) measures all of this, reading the FAB blackout share from fab.cooldown_windows.
decisions.evidence: No prototype had SIG, DOM, FAB or MEM. At every stamping act, FAB_COOLDOWN 400 blacks out FAB growth for about 20% of windows at a 2000-window cadence and about 27% at the union of 2000 and 3000 (arithmetic, 0b.1 item 16). Tree state: the act's shift stamp and DOM.on_retokenize are built (src/spine/loop.py around 1248-1254). The per-byte DOM levels and MEM's rescaled surprise (Q-MEM-14) are not built (TOK.Vocabulary.blen is still deferred, src/spine/compose.py:1634). fab.cooldown_windows does not exist in src. Decider: S5 (iii) (owed).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 27 (line 1390); 0b.1 item 2
decisions.question: Which data does codec readiness use?
decisions.options: The first media area in the schedule; '+generic' (D1's recipe: a declared generic set beside it)
decisions.current_recommendation: The first media area in the schedule. D1's recipe is the '+generic' arm (row 29).
decisions.evidence: This keeps later areas new to the codec, so codec BWT and arrival readings mean something.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 28 (line 1391); §13 decision rule ('The frozen controls are controls', line 1345)
decisions.question: How are live-vs-frozen comparisons made fair, and what happens if a frozen control wins?
decisions.options: Report step-matched and compute-matched frozen controls in every S5 plasticity cell; a winning frozen control goes to the owner; let a winning frozen control become the default automatically
decisions.current_recommendation: Every S5 plasticity cell reports step-matched and compute-matched frozen controls, labelled. A frozen control that wins goes to the owner as a 'necessary?' question and does not enter the default.
decisions.evidence: D3's mel gain was not step-matched (1500 vs +600 steps). D1's live vs frozen was not codec-step-matched (+308 steps) and not compute-matched (+20% wall). Bits/s is codec-dependent, so live vs frozen is judged on the codec-invariant primaries. Conflict built in: 'nothing frozen unless absolutely necessary' against 'performance decides'.

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 29 (line 1392); 0b.1 item 2 (recipe check, line 237); §13 S3 replica
decisions.question: Readiness recipe: how many codec steps, on what data, before media reaches the LM?
decisions.options: The first media area with at least 750 codec steps per candidate; '+generic' (D1's recipe, about 3000+ steps with a generic set)
decisions.current_recommendation: The first media area, at least 750 codec steps per candidate. '+generic' takes over if S3's readiness-only cell loses to D1 live25 by more than 2 paired SE on any primary.
decisions.evidence: D1's measured codec had 4000 steps and a generic pre-training set. The shipped default has neither, and nobody has measured that. Decider: S3 recipe check (owed).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 30 (line 1393); §12 cost deltas
decisions.question: What probe cost is affordable (cadence and n)?
decisions.options: Every 500 windows in readiness, then at every act ('snapshot') or every 500 windows ('jit_ema'), AUD_PROBE_N 400; sparser or smaller probes
decisions.current_recommendation: As stated; the GPU bench sets n and cadence.
decisions.evidence: On CPU one 400-clip reading costs about 11-14 s per area per codec (rev/probe_time.{py,txt}: 28-35 ms per clip, Griffin-Lim dominates; about 47 ms on another machine). Readiness probing: about 3.8 min at 500 against 36 s of D1 LM time, and about 9.5 min at 200. After readiness: about +71% of D1's LM time per arrived area, or +2.2-2.9% on R12's basis. Decider: GPU bench probe row (owed).

decisions.source: docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md §16 row 31 (line 1394); 0b.1 item 8
decisions.question: What is the ceiling guard's threshold?
decisions.options: Calibrated per family at S3 (the measured live-vs-frozen drop + 2 paired SE), count-only until then; a flat 0.05
decisions.current_recommendation: Calibrated per family at S3; count-only until calibrated.
decisions.evidence: A flat 0.05 would fire in the measured regime itself (D1 s0 drops 0.069 and 0.118) and put the refresh cadence into back-to-back holds of up to 4000 windows each. Decider: S3 calibration (owed).

Cadence c ships if bpb_c - bpb_0 <= M at EVERY seed; among those, the lower mean wins; if neither ships, 0 ships. Instrument: prequential bits/byte over the same bytes. Until the run, the tree keeps 3000 firing (Q-RUN-8 ruling), so runs past window 3000 change.
decisions.evidence: CPU equal-bytes check at seed 0 (scratch s0b/eq/s0_k0.json and s0_k1000.json): k0 2.6892 over 759,988 bytes in 4008 windows; k1000 2.6895 over 759,803 bytes in 3815 windows (4.8% fewer), 3 acts. Difference +0.0003. There is no nuisance control, so M is unknown; seed 1 did not complete. The earlier equal-window runs are not comparable (756,880 vs 795,938 bytes; c5768be). Archive: retok at 3000 gave held-out 4.364 b/B vs 2.175 at 0, but 22 of 23 retoks added zero tokens (src/tok/levers.py), which the act now refuses as a no-op. Owed: EXP=retok bash gpu_world.sh (k0, k3000, k1000, k0_nuis; seeds 0-2).

findings.claim: LR re-warming + LR re-decaying + replay of previous data matches fully re-training on all data (final loss and average LM-eval score), for a weak shift (English to English) and a strong shift (English to German) at 405M, and for a 10B model.
findings.source: Ibrahim, Therien et al. 2024, 'Simple and Scalable Strategies to Continually Pre-train Large Language Models', arXiv:2403.08763 (TMLR); abstract seen via search excerpt of the arXiv page
findings.numbers: 405M on hundreds of billions of tokens; 10B; matches the re-training baseline at a fraction of its compute
findings.implication: This is the default recipe for B's weight channel. The tree has replay (DATA rehearsal) and a re-warm lever (OPT_LR_SHIFT_WARM). It lacks a re-decay that does not need a known end. Owed: a joint i.i.d. re-train upper-bound arm against the continual arm on the owner's areas. 03 section 9 already names this arm.

findings.claim: The replay needed grows with the size of the shift: about 5% for a weak shift and about 25% for English to German. Re-warming the LR by itself causes some forgetting. The 10B model forgot less than the 405M one.
findings.source: Same paper (arXiv:2403.08763). The figures came from a secondary summary returned by search, not from the abstract or the PDF
findings.numbers: 5% (weak shift), ~25% (strong shift)
findings.implication: Replay rate should be a lever scaled by the measured shift, not one constant. The tree's measured 25-30% replay on modality addition (03 section 9) and the 27% self-regulation toy rate fall in the literature's strong-shift range. Confirm the figures in the PDF before quoting them as rulings.

findings.claim: Repeated cosine annealing, as used for large-scale continual pretraining, causes forgetting during each re-warming phase. The infinite learning-rate schedule is the more effective alternative, on image and language data, and needs no fixed iteration budget.
findings.source: Singh et al. 2025, 'Beyond Cosine Decay: On the effectiveness of Infinite Learning Rate Schedule for Continual Pre-training', arXiv:2503.02844 (ICML 2025); abstract via search excerpt
findings.numbers: qualitative (abstract)
findings.implication: CONFLICT with the tree defaults. OPT_LR_SCHED='cosine' with OPT_LR_RESTARTS=True fits a whole number of cycles to a known run length and re-warms each cycle. That serves neither 'after training' (no end date) nor 'without risking too much' (each re-warm forgets). Needed: a constant/WSD/infinite schedule arm under the same replay.

findings.claim: A constant LR plus a short cooldown scales as predictably as cosine and reaches about the same perplexity, so one long run can be cooled down from any checkpoint. Stochastic weight averaging improves models along the trajectory at no extra training cost.
findings.source: Hagele et al. 2024, 'Scaling Laws and Compute-Optimal Training Beyond Fixed Training Durations', arXiv:2405.18392 (NeurIPS 2024); abstract via search; official repo github.com/epfml/schedules-and-scaling read directly
findings.numbers: repo example cooldown fraction 0.2 of training (--wsd-fract-decay 0.2); SWA snapshot every 500 steps by default
findings.implication: This is the schedule shape for indefinite learning. The main line stays at a stable LR; a branch is cooled whenever a model must be evaluated or released. B comparisons must read cooled branches, or they are biased against the constant arm.

findings.claim: Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) splits training into warmup, stable and decay stages. It does not need the total number of training steps in advance, suits continuous training and domain adaptation, and makes intermediate checkpoints reusable.
findings.source: Hu et al. 2024, 'MiniCPM', arXiv:2404.06395 (COLM 2024); abstract via search
findings.numbers: MiniCPM 1.2B and 2.4B non-embedding parameters
findings.implication: A second candidate for the OPT schedule lever that has no end date.

findings.claim: Schedule-Free optimisation has no schedule and no stopping time, and gives state-of-the-art results across problems. It won the AlgoPerf 2024 self-tuning track. It still needs tuning.
findings.source: Defazio et al. 2024, 'The Road Less Scheduled', arXiv:2405.15682 (NeurIPS 2024); abstract via search; README of github.com/facebookresearch/schedule_free read directly
findings.numbers: README: beta 0.9 by default, 0.95-0.98 for long runs; AdamW LR 1-10x the scheduled rate; warmup recommended; BatchNorm and eval mode need care
findings.implication: A third schedule-free candidate arm. Its caveats (the beta for long runs, and the eval-mode switch that reads averaged weights) must be honoured, or the arm will read badly for the wrong reason.

findings.claim: MoE routers are robust to distribution shift during continual pretraining. MoEs continually pre-trained with replay and infinite LR schedules match a full re-training baseline, and are as good at CPT as a FLOP-matched dense model.
findings.source: Therien et al. 2025, 'Continual Pre-training of MoEs: How robust is your router?', arXiv:2503.05029 (TMLR 2025); abstract via search
findings.numbers: >2B-parameter Switch and DeepSeek MoE LLMs, 600B tokens, four MoE transformers
findings.implication: Expert routing is not a priori the weak point in B. But FAB is a growing fabric with learned routing and culls, unlike Switch or DeepSeek. Owed: a router-drift or imbalance gauge under a phase shift.

findings.claim: The stability gap: experience replay, constraint-based replay, distillation and parameter regularisation all forget heavily when a new task starts, then partly recover. The dip is invisible to evaluation at task ends only. It needs per-iteration evaluation and worst-case metrics.
findings.source: De Lange, van de Ven, Tuytelaars 2023, 'Continual evaluation for lifelong learning: Identifying the stability gap', arXiv:2205.13452 (ICLR 2023 spotlight); abstract via search
findings.numbers: qualitative; shown in class-, task- and domain-incremental benchmarks
findings.implication: Any held-out-probe gate in B must read continuously and hold a recovery window, or it will roll back healthy updates in the dip. A probe read only at phase ends misses the worst-case damage that the owner's 'without risking too much' is about.

findings.claim: LLM domain continual pretraining shows the same stability gap: a temporary drop, then slow recovery. Three things mitigate it: several epochs on a properly sized subset, a high-quality sub-corpus, and a mixture close to the pretraining data.
findings.source: Guo et al. 2024, 'Efficient Continual Pre-training by Mitigating the Stability Gap', arXiv:2406.14833 (ACL 2025); abstract via search
findings.numbers: OpenLlama-3B medical average 36.2% -> 40.7% at 40% of the original budget; Llama-3-8B, 5B medical tokens x 4 epochs
findings.implication: Consolidation phases should replay a mixture like the prior data and may repeat a small, high-quality set. Both are levers the DATA planner can express.

findings.claim: Catastrophic forgetting appears in 1B-7B LLMs during continual instruction tuning. It gets worse with scale in that range. Decoder-only BLOOMZ forgets less than mT0. General instruction tuning first reduces later forgetting.
findings.source: Luo et al. 2023, arXiv:2308.08747 (IEEE/ACM TASLP 2025); abstract via search
findings.numbers: 1B to 7B
findings.implication: This conflicts with the secondary report that 10B forgets less than 405M in CPT. Scale direction is unsettled, so toy-scale forgetting verdicts are signals, not definitives.

findings.claim: Forgetting during fine-tuning follows a shifted power law in the number of parameters fine-tuned and the number of update steps. LoRA still forgets. Fine-tuning gain and forgetting are strongly inversely linear, and neither early stopping nor fewer tuned parameters avoids forgetting.
findings.source: Kalajdzievski 2024, 'Scaling Laws for Forgetting When Fine-Tuning Large Language Models', arXiv:2401.05605; abstract via search
findings.numbers: Llama 2 7B chat; knowledge, reasoning and safety guardrails affected
findings.implication: Every post-training weight update pays a forgetting price that grows with how much it learns. Bounded risk therefore needs budgets on steps and touched parameters plus replay, not only regularisers.

findings.claim: LoRA substantially underperforms full fine-tuning on the target domain but keeps more out-of-domain performance than weight decay or dropout do. Full fine-tuning learns perturbations of 10-100x higher rank.
findings.source: Biderman et al. 2024, 'LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less', arXiv:2405.09673 (TMLR 2024); abstract via search
findings.numbers: code and math; ~100K instruction pairs and 20B-token CPT regimes; rank 10-100x
findings.implication: Low-rank or adapter updates are a middle-risk tier: less learning for less forgetting. It is a dial, not a free lunch.

findings.claim: Sparse memory finetuning updates only memory-layer slots that new knowledge activates strongly. At the same new-knowledge acquisition it forgets far less than full fine-tuning or LoRA.
findings.source: Lin et al. 2025, 'Continual Learning via Sparse Memory Finetuning', arXiv:2510.15103; abstract via search
findings.numbers: NaturalQuestions F1 drop: 89% full FT, 71% LoRA, 11% sparse memory FT
findings.implication: This is the strongest recent evidence that slot-addressed sparse parameter updates are the low-risk weight channel. It is the closest literature analogue to FAB slots and MEM. It favours routing post-training learning into slots rather than the dense core.

findings.claim: Continual-T0 learns 8 new, diverse generation tasks and keeps performance across 70 datasets. It uses rehearsal of a small share of previous data. Self-supervised pretraining is what makes LMs continual learners.
findings.source: Scialom et al. 2022, 'Fine-tuned Language Models are Continual Learners', arXiv:2205.12393 (EMNLP 2022); abstract via search
findings.numbers: 8 tasks, 70 datasets; rehearsal of about 1% (the 1% figure was in a search excerpt, not confirmed in the abstract)
findings.implication: Instruction-level continual learning needs little rehearsal. Replay can be small when the new material is task-like rather than a distribution shift.

findings.claim: Replaying generic pretraining data during fine-tuning improves the TARGET task, not only retention. The gain is larger when little target data was present in pretraining.
findings.source: Kotha and Liang 2026, 'Replaying pre-training data improves fine-tuning', arXiv:2603.04964; abstract via search
findings.numbers: 150M models, 4M target tokens, 4B total; target data efficiency up to 1.87x (fine-tuning) and 2.06x (mid-training)
findings.implication: Replay after training is not a tax on learning; it can speed it. This supports replay ON by default in every post-training learning phase.

findings.claim: Spaced Repetition Training schedules which examples are rehearsed with the SM-2 algorithm. On Wikipedia and code corpora split by time it recovers far more old knowledge than naive CPT, keeps or improves new learning, and at larger scale keeps broad benchmarks that naive CPT and uniform replay degrade.
findings.source: arXiv:2608.17530 (2026), 'When to Review: Spaced Repetition for Continual Pre-Training of Language Models'; abstract via search
findings.numbers: recovers 5-37 percentage points of old-knowledge accuracy lost by naive CPT
findings.implication: Supports the tree's retention-paced rehearsal (proposal 04). The tree's toy result that it ties a fixed 27% replay may not hold at scale. The GPU E1 experiment stays the decider.

findings.claim: RL and SFT reach similar new-task performance, but RL keeps prior abilities much better. Forgetting is set by the KL divergence between the fine-tuned and base policy, measured on the new task. On-policy updates are biased toward KL-minimal solutions.
findings.source: Shenfeld et al. 2025, 'RL's Razor: Why Online Reinforcement Learning Forgets Less', arXiv:2509.04259; abstract via search
findings.numbers: LLMs and robotic foundation models
findings.implication: This gives B a cheap forgetting PREDICTOR to gate on: KL to the anchor model on the new data. It also suggests targets the model generates itself (on-policy) are lower-risk material to learn from than off-policy text.

findings.claim: Test-time training on nearest neighbours retrieves about 20 neighbours from a Pile index for each test input and fine-tunes one gradient step on each. It improves more than 20 Pile language-modelling tasks and closes much of the gap between GPT-2 and a GPT-Neo over 10x larger.
findings.source: Hardt and Sun 2024, 'Test-Time Training on Nearest Neighbors for Large Language Models', arXiv:2305.18466 (ICLR 2024); abstract via search
findings.numbers: 20 neighbours, 1 step each; >20 tasks; >10x size gap narrowed
findings.implication: Retrieval plus temporary per-input updates is an adaptation tier that leaves no lasting change. Whether the paper resets weights per input was not confirmed this session.

findings.claim: Test-time training temporarily updates parameters at inference. It gives up to 6x accuracy for small models and 53% on the ARC public validation set with a purely neural approach, 61.9% when ensembled with program synthesis. It needs prior fine-tuning on similar tasks, an auxiliary task format with augmentations, and per-instance training.
findings.source: Akyurek et al. 2024, 'The Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training for Few-Shot Learning', arXiv:2411.07279; abstract via search
findings.implication: Temporary updates carry zero persistent risk. The tree has no evaluation-time adaptation lever; it is owed as a T0 tier.

findings.claim: Dynamic evaluation adapts a sequence model to recent history by gradient descent at evaluation time.
findings.source: Krause et al. 2018, 'Dynamic Evaluation of Neural Sequence Models', arXiv:1709.07432 (ICML 2018); Transformer-XL follow-up arXiv:1904.08378; via search
findings.numbers: PTB 51.1, WikiText-2 44.3 perplexity; text8 1.19, Hutter 1.08 bits/char; Transformer-XL enwik8 0.99 -> 0.94 bits/char
findings.implication: This is the classic online-learning result for LMs. Its gains come at inference with local adaptation. Applies to the tree's byte-level bits/byte metric directly.

findings.claim: kNN-LM interpolates an LM with a nearest-neighbour model over a datastore of its own embeddings. It improves perplexity with no training and adapts to a domain by swapping the datastore.
findings.source: Khandelwal et al. 2020, 'Generalization through Memorization: Nearest Neighbor Language Models', arXiv:1911.00172 (ICLR 2020); abstract via search
findings.numbers: WikiText-103 perplexity 15.79, a 2.9-point improvement, no additional training
findings.implication: This is the memory channel as the low-risk learning path: no weight change, and entries can be deleted. It is the literature basis for MEM (MEM_BLEND_MAX 0.5).

findings.claim: RETRO conditions on chunks retrieved from a 2-trillion-token database. It matches GPT-3 and Jurassic-1 on the Pile with 25x fewer parameters.
findings.source: Borgeaud et al. 2022, arXiv:2112.04426 (ICML 2022); abstract via search
findings.numbers: 2T-token database; 25x fewer parameters
findings.implication: External memory can stand in for parameters at scale. Knowledge added after training can live in the database, not the weights.

findings.claim: For knowledge injection, RAG consistently beats unsupervised fine-tuning, for both knowledge seen in training and new knowledge. LLMs struggle to learn new facts through unsupervised fine-tuning; many paraphrases of the same fact help.
findings.source: Ovadia et al. 2024, 'Fine-Tuning or Retrieval? Comparing Knowledge Injection in LLMs', arXiv:2312.05934 (EMNLP 2024); abstract via search
findings.numbers: qualitative (abstract)
findings.implication: Put new facts in memory first. Move them into weights later only with paraphrase augmentation and gates.

findings.claim: GRACE writes spot-fixes for streaming errors into a discrete local codebook in the latent space, without changing weights. It is the first method to make thousands of sequential edits from streaming errors alone, with little effect on unrelated inputs.
findings.source: Hartvigsen et al. 2023, 'Aging with GRACE', arXiv:2211.11031 (NeurIPS 2023); abstract via search
findings.numbers: thousands of sequential edits; T5, BERT, GPT
findings.implication: Key-value adapters are the safe form of model editing and are structurally similar to MEM. Weight editing is not (next finding).

findings.claim: Sequential ROME/MEMIT editing makes a model steadily less editable. It forgets earlier edits and loses downstream ability, first gradually and then catastrophically.
findings.source: Gupta, Rao, Anumanchipalli 2024, 'Model Editing at Scale leads to Gradual and Catastrophic Forgetting', arXiv:2401.07453 (Findings of ACL 2024); abstract via search
findings.numbers: two phases: gradual, then abrupt
findings.implication: Do not use locate-and-edit weight editing as a post-training learning channel.

findings.claim: Unlearning is not a reliable undo. Fine-tuning on 10 unrelated examples, or removing specific activation directions, recovers most supposedly unlearned hazardous capability.
findings.source: Lucki et al. 2024, 'An Adversarial Perspective on Machine Unlearning for AI Safety', arXiv:2409.18025; abstract via search
findings.numbers: after 10 retain-set samples: accuracy 61.6% (RMU), 57.0% (DPO), 52.7% (NPO)
findings.implication: Reversibility in B must come from checkpoints, weight interpolation and memory deletion, not gradient unlearning. This matches the tree's cl_bench.py thesis: local, cheap memory deletion vs expensive unlearning with collateral.

findings.claim: WiSE-FT linearly interpolates the weights of a zero-shot and a fine-tuned model. It raises accuracy under distribution shift while keeping target accuracy, at no extra cost.
findings.source: Wortsman et al. 2022, 'Robust fine-tuning of zero-shot models', arXiv:2109.01903 (CVPR 2022); abstract via search
findings.numbers: +4 to +6 pp on ImageNet shifts; +2 to +23 pp on six further shifts
findings.implication: This gives a GRADED rollback: interpolate toward the anchor checkpoint instead of reverting all the way. It is cheap and needs only a stored anchor.

findings.claim: A 'negative flip' is a sample the old model got right and the new one gets wrong. The negative flip rate (NFR) measures regressions between versions. Focal distillation reduces flips while lowering error.
findings.source: Yan et al. 2021, 'Positive-Congruent Training: Towards Regression-Free Model Updates', arXiv:2011.09161 (CVPR 2021); abstract via search
findings.numbers: NFR = fraction of samples correct before and wrong after
findings.implication: A promotion gate should read per-probe regressions (negative flips per area or item), not only the mean loss. A mean can improve while specific skills break.

findings.claim: In continual settings, standard deep learning slowly loses plasticity until it learns no better than a shallow network. Continual backprop reinitialises a small fraction of less-used units. L2 regularisation eases the loss, especially with weight perturbation. Dropout and batch norm do not prevent it.
findings.source: Dohare et al. 2024, 'Loss of plasticity in deep continual learning', Nature 632:768-774; via search
findings.numbers: qualitative across architectures, optimisers and activations
findings.implication: Learning indefinitely needs active plasticity maintenance. The tree cites this for FAB slot reuse (contract ~2909). A plasticity PROBE is still owed: learning speed on a fresh area measured late in a run.

findings.claim: Warm-starting from previous weights generalises worse than training from scratch, even on stationary data. Shrink-and-perturb (shrink the weights toward zero, then add small noise) fixes this.
findings.source: Ash and Adams 2020, 'On Warm-Starting Neural Network Training', arXiv:1910.08475 (NeurIPS 2020); via search
findings.numbers: qualitative
findings.implication: A perturbation-based plasticity remedy. It is structurally close to FAB_MUT and FAB_BIRTH_JITTER at expert birth, but applied to existing weights.

findings.claim: L2 Init, an L2 penalty toward the initial parameters rather than the origin, mitigates plasticity loss most consistently across kinds of nonstationarity, with a single hyperparameter.
findings.source: Kumar et al. 2023/2025, 'Maintaining Plasticity in Continual Learning via Regenerative Regularization', arXiv:2308.11958 (CoLLAs, PMLR v274); abstract via search
findings.numbers: one hyperparameter
findings.implication: A cheap plasticity lever. It can combine with the tree's existing anchor idea (LM_ANCHOR_W holds new rows near their composite).

findings.claim: Loss of plasticity breaks down into several independent mechanisms. Fixing any one alone is not enough, but layer normalisation combined with weight decay is highly effective.
findings.source: Lyle et al. 2024, 'Disentangling the Causes of Plasticity Loss in Neural Networks', arXiv:2402.18762 (CoLLAs, PMLR v274); abstract via search
findings.numbers: synthetic nonstationary tasks and the Arcade Learning Environment
findings.implication: CONFLICT with a tree default: OPT_WEIGHT_DECAY=0.0 is the plasticity-risk setting. Owed: a weight-decay arm read on a late plasticity probe as well as final bits/byte.

findings.claim: Larger weight decay in pretraining makes the model more plastic, so it gains more from later fine-tuning. A base model that is worse after pretraining can be better after further training.
findings.source: Han, Bordt, Zhang, Kakade 2026, 'Weight Decay Improves Language Model Plasticity', arXiv:2602.11137; abstract via search
findings.numbers: qualitative (abstract)
findings.implication: The owner's rule that 'performance is the deciding factor' must count performance AFTER further learning, not only end-of-run loss, when B is the priority. Otherwise the tree can choose settings that lose plasticity.

findings.claim: GPT-style transformers lose plasticity on a multilingual continual-learning problem, measured as worse learning on a held-out Vietnamese probe. The onset follows a predictable scaling law that grows sublinearly with model size.
findings.source: arXiv:2606.24752 (2026), 'Can Scale Save Us From Plasticity Loss in Large Language Models?'; abstract via search
findings.numbers: 5M to 314M non-embedding parameters
findings.implication: Plasticity loss is real in the tree's size range, and scale only delays it. Owed: a plasticity probe, a new-area learning curve read at intervals.

findings.claim: Plasticity loss is largely an artefact of abrupt task changes. It is mostly avoided when the environment changes gradually, through interpolated inputs or outputs or task sampling.
findings.source: Liu and Mou 2026, 'Do Neural Networks Lose Plasticity in a Gradually Changing World?', arXiv:2602.09234; abstract via search
findings.numbers: four benchmarks
findings.implication: This favours the tree's rehearsed sliding-window phase schedule over pure-add. Abrupt phase switches are the worst case for both forgetting and plasticity.

findings.claim: Deep RL agents overfit to early experience (primacy bias). Periodically resetting the last layers while keeping the replay buffer improves Atari 100k and DeepMind Control results.
findings.source: Nikishin et al. 2022, 'The Primacy Bias in Deep Reinforcement Learning', arXiv:2205.07802 (ICML 2022); abstract via search
findings.numbers: Atari 100k; DMC
findings.implication: A reset is safe only when a memory or replay store holds what the reset part knew. Pair any reset or cull lever with replay.

findings.claim: Training generative models indiscriminately on model-generated content causes irreversible defects: the tails of the original distribution disappear. This holds for LLMs, VAEs and GMMs.
findings.source: Shumailov et al. 2024, 'AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data', Nature 631:755-759; via search
findings.numbers: qualitative
findings.implication: Learning from its own outputs after deployment is a collapse risk. Self-generated material must be tagged and never replace real data.

findings.claim: Replacing real data with each generation's synthetic data leads toward collapse. Accumulating synthetic data alongside the original real data avoids it.
findings.source: Gerstgrasser et al. 2024, 'Is Model Collapse Inevitable?', arXiv:2404.01413; abstract via search
findings.numbers: sequences of LMs pretrained on text corpora
findings.implication: Keep the original data forever as a replay anchor, and accumulate rather than replace. This argues against any eviction policy that removes the last copy of real data.

findings.claim: Split-view and frontrunning attacks make poisoning web-scale datasets practical.
findings.source: Carlini et al. 2024, 'Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical', arXiv:2302.10149 (IEEE S&P 2024); abstract via search
findings.numbers: 0.01% of LAION-400M or COYO-700M for $60; 10 popular datasets affected
findings.implication: Untrusted post-training inputs are an active attack surface. Provenance, meaning which source and when, is a first-class requirement.

findings.claim: Poisoning needs a nearly CONSTANT number of documents, whatever the size of the model or dataset.
findings.source: Souly et al. 2025, 'Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-constant Number of Poison Samples', arXiv:2510.07192 (Anthropic, UK AISI, Turing, OATML); abstract via search
findings.numbers: 250 poisoned documents compromise models from 600M to 13B trained on Chinchilla-optimal data (6B to 260B tokens), although the largest see over 20x more clean data
findings.implication: Dilution is not a defence. B needs per-source caps and rate limits on what any one source can write to memory or push into weights, plus quarantine and corroboration before promotion.

findings.claim: Poisoning 0.1% of pretraining data is enough for 3 of 4 attack types to persist through SFT and DPO. Denial-of-service is effective and persistent from 0.001%.
findings.source: Zhang et al. 2025, 'Persistent Pre-Training Poisoning of LLMs', arXiv:2410.13722 (ICLR 2025); via search excerpts
findings.numbers: 600M to 7B; 0.1% for 3 of 4 attacks; DoS from 0.001%; Wikipedia tampering could reach 0.27% of the OLMo pretraining set
findings.implication: Poison that reaches weights survives later training. Gate content before it reaches weights, not after.

findings.claim: About 100 poison examples in instruction-tuning data make a trigger phrase force negative polarity or degenerate output across hundreds of held-out tasks. Larger LMs are more vulnerable. Filtering and capacity reduction give only moderate protection and cost accuracy.
findings.source: Wan, Wallace, Shen, Klein 2023, 'Poisoning Language Models During Instruction Tuning', arXiv:2305.00944 (ICML 2023); abstract via search
findings.numbers: about 100 examples
findings.implication: Filtering alone does not bound the risk. Canary or trigger probes and source-level limits are needed in addition.

findings.claim: Backdoored deceptive behaviour can persist through supervised fine-tuning, RL and adversarial training. It persists most in the largest models, and adversarial training can teach the model to hide its trigger.
findings.source: Hubinger et al. 2024, 'Sleeper Agents', arXiv:2401.05566; abstract via search
findings.numbers: qualitative
findings.implication: Removal after the fact is unreliable. Prevention and rollback to a pre-contamination checkpoint are the only dependable controls.

findings.claim: Tay, a chatbot that learned from Twitter users, was taken offline about 16 hours after launch following a coordinated attack that exploited a 'repeat after me' behaviour.
findings.source: Tay (chatbot) incident, March 23-24 2016; Wikipedia, TIME and TechCrunch pages via search
findings.numbers: about 16 hours; about 96,000 tweets
findings.implication: This is the canonical warning for 'learning after training' from open input with no gate, trust model or rollback.

findings.claim: Deep Partition Aggregation trains base models on hash-determined partitions of the training set and aggregates their votes. This certifies robustness against a bounded number of inserted or deleted training samples.
findings.source: Levine and Feizi 2021, 'Deep Partition Aggregation', arXiv:2006.14768 (ICLR 2021); abstract via search
findings.numbers: certified per-sample bound (classification)
findings.implication: Partitioning influence by source bounds what any one source can do. DOM/FAB/MEM ownership by source is the tree-native analogue. No certificate exists for LMs; any benefit here is a measurement owed.

findings.claim: Complementary learning systems: a sparse, pattern-separated hippocampus learns episodes fast; a distributed neocortex integrates slowly across episodes; recent memories are replayed to consolidate them.
findings.source: McClelland, McNaughton, O'Reilly 1995, Psychological Review 102:419-457; via search (PubMed / publisher)
findings.numbers: n/a (theory)
findings.implication: This is the architectural template B converges on: fast memory (MEM), slow weights (LM/FAB), and replay-based consolidation in gated phases.

findings.claim: Elastic weight consolidation protects weights important to earlier tasks with a quadratic penalty.
findings.source: Kirkpatrick et al. 2017, PNAS 114(13):3521-3526; via search
findings.numbers: n/a
findings.implication: A regulariser-only defence. By De Lange 2023, parameter regularisation still shows the stability gap, so it is a complement to replay, not a substitute.

findings.claim: In the tree's one real continual-learning run (English, then Python), English held, but every English memory entry was evicted during the Python phases. Memory's contribution was negative, and retention came from weights and the fabric.
findings.source: LLM-Test notes/01_TIMELINE.md, row 08-14 (commit a9d7258); read this session
findings.numbers: eng 1.998 -> 2.050 (+0.052 +/- 0.075, HELD); fabric +0.373 b/B; memory -0.111 b/B; n=1, no seed replication
findings.implication: Memory is the lowest-risk WRITE channel but not yet a demonstrated RETENTION channel in this tree. Per-source floors (MEM_SRC_SHARE) came later. Owed: a phased run with the floor on, reporting memory's per-area contribution.

findings.claim: Dropout randomly removes units and their connections during training, which prevents co-adaptation and reduces overfitting. It improved supervised tasks in vision, speech, document classification and computational biology.
findings.source: Srivastava et al. 2014, JMLR 15:1929-1958; via search
findings.numbers: qualitative (abstract)
findings.implication: This is the founding FOR case: deliberately making units unreliable improves generalisation, in the multi-epoch, overfitting-prone regime.

findings.claim: In single-epoch LM pretraining, dropout HURTS. BERT and Pythia models trained without dropout do better downstream, and 'early dropout' is also worse than none. Models trained without dropout are also easier to edit by gradient-based methods (MEND).
findings.source: Liu, Bauer, Manning 2025, 'Drop Dropout on Single-Epoch Language Model Pretraining', arXiv:2505.24788 (Findings of ACL 2025); abstract via search
findings.numbers: Pythia 160M and 1.4B; LM, BLiMP, SQuAD, MNLI all better without dropout
findings.implication: This is the AGAINST case in the data-rich single-pass regime. The tree's LM_DROPOUT=0.0 default fits it at RUN_EPOCHS 1. After training, replay repeats data and moves toward the regime where noise helps, so the dropout verdict can flip between phases. That argues for a phase-scheduled lever.

findings.claim: Training on sampled alternative segmentations (subword regularisation) gives consistent gains, especially in low-resource and out-of-domain settings.
findings.source: Kudo 2018, 'Subword Regularization', ACL 2018 (P18-1007), arXiv:1804.10959; abstract via search
findings.numbers: qualitative (abstract)
findings.implication: Segmentation unreliability helps most exactly where generalisation is hardest: little data and out-of-domain input. This is direct precedent for TOK_DROPOUT and retokenisation churn.

findings.claim: BPE-dropout randomly skips merges during training and uses standard BPE at inference. It raises translation quality over BPE and over earlier subword regularisation.
findings.source: Provilkov, Emelianenko, Voita 2020, 'BPE-Dropout', arXiv:1910.13267 (ACL 2020); abstract via search
findings.numbers: up to +2.3 BLEU over BPE; up to +0.9 BLEU over subword regularisation
findings.implication: The closest precedent to the tree's TOK_DROPOUT, which also skips available merges. It supports trying the lever on, read against held-out bits/byte, and says nothing about single-pass LM pretraining at scale.

findings.claim: StochasTok randomly splits tokens during pretraining. It works with any base tokenizer or pretrained model and substantially improves subword-level tasks such as character counting and substring identification.
findings.source: Sims et al. 2025/2026, 'StochasTok', arXiv:2506.01687 (ICLR 2026); abstract via search
findings.numbers: qualitative (abstract)
findings.implication: Segmentation noise buys fine-grained structure awareness cheaply. Useful when the segmentation itself keeps changing, as with live retokenisation.

findings.claim: Models trained only on canonical tokenisation still handle non-canonical tokenisations never seen in training. Robustness grows with model strength and falls as the tokenisation departs further from canonical.
findings.source: Zheng et al. 2025, 'Broken Tokens? Your Language Model can Secretly Handle Non-Canonical Tokenizations', arXiv:2506.19004; abstract via search
findings.numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct keeps 93.4% of performance with random tokenisation and 90.8% at character level; character-level segmentation improves string tasks up to 15%
findings.implication: Tokenisation churn after training (live retok) is survivable even without training on it. Training with it (TOK_DROPOUT) should close the remaining gap. Measure the retok cost directly as bits/byte before and after an act.

findings.claim: Stochastic depth randomly drops residual blocks during training and bypasses them with the identity. It lets very deep ResNets train and improve, and cuts training time.
findings.source: Huang et al. 2016, 'Deep Networks with Stochastic Depth', arXiv:1603.09382 (ECCV 2016); via search
findings.numbers: 1202-layer ResNet 4.91% CIFAR-10 test error with it; without it 7.93%, worse than 110 layers
findings.implication: Unreliable depth is a working regulariser. It is the analogue of the tree's FAB halting and ponder depth being stochastic.

findings.claim: NEFTune adds noise to the embedding vectors during instruction fine-tuning and substantially improves conversational quality.
findings.source: Jain et al. 2023, 'NEFTune: Noisy Embeddings Improve Instruction Finetuning', arXiv:2310.05914 (ICLR 2024); abstract via search
findings.numbers: LLaMA-2-7B on Alpaca: AlpacaEval 29.79% -> 64.69%
findings.implication: Strong FOR evidence in the small-data, multi-epoch fine-tuning regime, which is the regime of post-training learning on small new data.

findings.claim: Noisy Student self-trains an equal-or-larger student with noise (dropout, stochastic depth, augmentation) on teacher pseudo-labels. It improves accuracy and robustness at the same time.
findings.source: Xie et al. 2020, 'Self-training with Noisy Student improves ImageNet classification', CVPR 2020 (arXiv:1911.04252); via search
findings.numbers: 88.4% top-1 (+2.0 over the prior SOTA); ImageNet-A 61.0% -> 83.7%; ImageNet-C mCE 45.7 -> 28.3; ImageNet-P mean flip rate 27.8 -> 12.2
findings.implication: Noise combined with self-generated targets and MORE data generalises. It is a self-training loop that works because noise stops the student copying the teacher, and because real labelled data stays in the mix.

findings.claim: Domain randomisation trains a detector only on simulated images with non-realistic random textures, varied enough that the real world looks like one more variation. It transfers to reality.
findings.source: Tobin et al. 2017, arXiv:1703.06907 (IROS 2017); abstract via search
findings.numbers: real-world object localisation accurate to 1.5 cm, robust to distractors and partial occlusion
findings.implication: FOR the belief: enough variability in nuisance factors forces invariant features. The condition is breadth: reality must fall inside the randomised range.

findings.claim: Automatic domain randomisation (ADR) generates environments of ever-increasing difficulty and greatly improves sim-to-real transfer. Memory-augmented policies trained on ADR show emergent meta-learning at test time.
findings.source: OpenAI et al. 2019, 'Solving Rubik's Cube with a Robot Hand', arXiv:1910.07113; abstract via search
findings.numbers: qualitative (abstract)
findings.implication: The closest precedent for the owner's belief in its strongest form: self-regulated unreliability plus memory leads to emergent adaptation. It is also a self-regulation mechanism. An ADR-style noise controller is a natural arm, with a fixed noise ladder as its control.

findings.claim: In-context learning emerges when training data is bursty and has many rare classes, and more strongly when item meanings are dynamic rather than fixed.
findings.source: Chan et al. 2022, 'Data Distributional Properties Drive Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers', arXiv:2205.05055 (NeurIPS 2022); abstract via search
findings.numbers: qualitative (abstract)
findings.implication: Unreliable MAPPINGS (the same symbol meaning different things in different contexts) push models toward in-context adaptation. Testable in the tree with a synthetic 'dynamic meaning' area whose key-to-value map changes per segment.

findings.claim: There is a task-diversity threshold. Below it, a pretrained transformer cannot solve unseen regression tasks and behaves like a Bayesian estimator with the narrow pretraining prior. Above it, it behaves like ridge regression and generalises to unseen tasks.
findings.source: Raventos, Paul, Chen, Ganguli 2023, arXiv:2306.15063 (NeurIPS 2023); via search
findings.numbers: sharp threshold (value task-dependent)
findings.implication: Variability forces generalisation only above a threshold. Below it, the variability is memorised. Any tree test must sweep the diversity or unreliability level, not test one setting.

findings.claim: Meta-trained transformers pass through phases, from instance memorisation to system identification to general learning, as model size and the number of tasks grow. Capability is limited by the size of the state (memory) the prediction can use.
findings.source: Kirsch et al. 2022, 'General-Purpose In-Context Learning by Meta-Learning Transformers', arXiv:2212.04458; abstract via search
findings.numbers: phase transitions in model size and task count
findings.implication: Generalisation from variability needs enough capacity AND enough memory. This links the belief to MEM and context length and warns that toy scale may sit below the transition.

findings.claim: CLIP's robustness to distribution shift comes mainly from its more diverse training distribution. Training-set size, language supervision and the contrastive loss contribute little or nothing.
findings.source: Fang et al. 2022, 'Data Determines Distributional Robustness in CLIP', arXiv:2205.01397 (ICML 2022); abstract via search
findings.numbers: five candidate causes tested; diversity is the main one
findings.implication: 'Robustness from diversity' is supported; 'robustness from noise' less so. The tree's lever is data breadth (areas, sources), not only noise level.

findings.claim: DNNs trained on a given image distortion exceed humans on that distortion but generalise extremely poorly to other distortions. For example, training on salt-and-pepper noise does not give robustness to uniform white noise.
findings.source: Geirhos et al. 2018, 'Generalisation in humans and deep neural networks', arXiv:1808.08750 (NeurIPS 2018); abstract via search
findings.numbers: 12 degradation types; ResNet-152, VGG-19, GoogLeNet
findings.implication: AGAINST the broad form of the belief. Robustness learned from one kind of unreliability does not carry over to another. The decisive tree test holds out a whole perturbation family.

findings.claim: Character-based NMT fails on moderately noisy text that humans read easily. Structure-invariant representations and training on noisy text improve robustness, and a character-CNN model can become robust to several noise kinds at once.
findings.source: Belinkov and Bisk 2018, 'Synthetic and Natural Noise Both Break Neural Machine Translation', arXiv:1711.02173 (ICLR 2018); abstract via search
findings.numbers: qualitative (abstract)
findings.implication: Mixed-noise training can give multi-noise robustness, but only for the noise kinds included. That supports mixing several unreliability families, not one.

findings.claim: CNNs trained with SGD easily fit random labels and even pure random-noise images, and explicit regularisation does not change this qualitatively.
findings.source: Zhang et al. 2017, 'Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization', arXiv:1611.03530 (ICLR 2017); via search
findings.numbers: qualitative
findings.implication: AGAINST: capacity memorises unreliability rather than being forced past it. Noise that is not zero-mean relative to the target becomes content.

findings.claim: Networks learn simple patterns before memorising noise. Well-tuned explicit regularisation such as dropout can slow the fitting of noise without hurting generalisation on real data.
findings.source: Arpit et al. 2017, 'A Closer Look at Memorization in Deep Networks', arXiv:1706.05394 (ICML 2017); abstract via search
findings.numbers: qualitative
findings.implication: Regime nuance: early in training, and with regularisation, unreliable items are learned last or not at all. Late or unregularised training memorises them. Timing and regularisation set the outcome.

findings.claim: Deep networks generalise from data where correct labels are massively outnumbered by random ones, but this needs a large increase in dataset size tied to the dilution factor. Larger batches help because the noisy gradients cancel.
findings.source: Rolnick et al. 2017, 'Deep Learning is Robust to Massive Label Noise', arXiv:1705.10694; abstract via search
findings.numbers: MNIST >90% test accuracy with 100 random-label examples per clean example
findings.implication: Tolerance exists but is paid for in data and compute, a cost the owner's 'performance decides' must charge to the noisy arm.

findings.claim: With symmetric label noise, test accuracy is a quadratic function of the noise ratio.
findings.source: Chen et al. 2019, 'Understanding and Utilizing Deep Neural Networks Trained with Noisy Labels', arXiv:1905.05040 (ICML 2019); via search
findings.numbers: accuracy quadratic in noise ratio (symmetric noise)
findings.implication: AGAINST for target corruption: there is no sweet spot, only a monotone cost. Unreliable TARGETS differ from unreliable INPUTS.

findings.claim: Label noise produces double descent over model size and training time, and in some regimes 4x more training data makes test performance worse.
findings.source: Nakkiran et al. 2020, 'Deep Double Descent', arXiv:1912.02292 (ICLR 2020; J. Stat. Mech. 2021); via search
findings.numbers: CIFAR-10 with 15% label noise
findings.implication: Unreliability creates non-monotone, unstable regimes, so a single-setting test can mislead. Sweep levels and training length.

findings.claim: Adversarial robustness and standard accuracy can conflict. Robust models learn different features and can lose clean accuracy.
findings.source: Tsipras et al. 2019, 'Robustness May Be at Odds with Accuracy', arXiv:1805.12152 (ICLR 2019); abstract via search
findings.numbers: provable in a simple natural setting
findings.implication: Robustness to worst-case unreliability has a clean-performance price. Performance must be read on clean held-out data as well as perturbed data.

findings.claim: Junk data sharply reduces how much useful knowledge a model can store, but prepending a domain name or source token to useful data restores the capacity. Models store about 2 bits of knowledge per parameter.
findings.source: Allen-Zhu and Li 2024/2025, 'Physics of Language Models: Part 3.3, Knowledge Capacity Scaling Laws', arXiv:2404.05405 (ICLR 2025); via search excerpts. The 20x figure comes from a secondary summary
findings.numbers: ~2 bits/parameter; up to ~20x less knowledge when useful data is 1/8 of tokens and junk 7/8 (secondary); about 1000 exposures per fact for full capacity
findings.implication: Unreliable content is harmful unless it can be ATTRIBUTED. This supports source tags (DATA_TAG) as the enabling condition for learning safely from mixed-reliability sources.

findings.claim: MeCo pretrains with metadata such as URLs prepended, then runs a cooldown on plain text so the model works without metadata. It speeds up pretraining.
findings.source: Gao et al. 2025, 'Metadata Conditioning Accelerates Language Model Pre-training', arXiv:2501.01956 (ICML 2025); abstract via search
findings.numbers: a 1.6B model matches standard pretraining with 33% less data; effect shown from 600M to 8B on C4, RefinedWeb, DCLM
findings.implication: Source identity is a cheap accelerator and the cooldown keeps the untagged read working. The tree's tag channel with tag dropout is a per-token variant.

findings.claim: On long-tailed distributions, memorising labels, including rare and atypical ones, is necessary for close-to-optimal generalisation.
findings.source: Feldman 2020, 'Does Learning Require Memorization? A Short Tale about a Long Tail', arXiv:1906.05271 (STOC 2020); via search
findings.numbers: theory
findings.implication: Rare-but-true items look like unreliability. Filtering or noise-hardening that discards them costs accuracy, so rare items should be held (for example in memory) rather than washed out.

findings.claim: In-tree: making the source tag unreliable (dropped on 25% of segments) is what lets the model work without the tag. With no tag dropout, the untagged read is much worse.
findings.source: LLM-Test docs/proposals/04_SELF_REGULATION.md section 9 (d2 prototype, 5 seeds); read this session
findings.numbers: untagged mean6 at DATA_TAG_DROP 0.25: 1.585 / 1.656 / 1.317; at drop 0: 2.246 / 2.214 / 2.064 bits/byte. Tagged read 1.352-1.481 vs planned 1.621-1.751; untagged vs planned -0.015 / +0.092 / +0.049 / +0.092 / +0.037
findings.implication: In-tree support for the narrow (invariance) form of the belief: an unreliable cue stops over-reliance on it. There is still a small cost versus never tagging at 4 of 5 seeds. Toy scale; a signal.

findings.claim: In-tree: a live (drifting) codec lowers LM bits/s against a frozen codec, but the LM-side codec-invariant readings show no consistent gain. Timbre recovery falls at high plasticity.
findings.source: LLM-Test docs/proposals/03b_LIVE_CODEC.md rows 1, 4, 15 (D1/D3 prototypes); read this session
findings.numbers: bits/s lower 24/24 (-0.93 to -7.76; codec-dependent metric); caption bits/byte worse 11 of 16; B understanding exact worse 5 of 8; generation exact worse 12 of 32, better 18; D3 high-plasticity tones timbre lower 4 of 4
findings.implication: In-tree evidence that representation drift, a form of unreliability, did NOT clearly produce better invariant generalisation at toy scale. The belief is inconclusive here, not supported.

findings.claim: In-tree: credibility inside the model did not emerge without a tag. Learning-progress focus with no trust mechanism drew MORE from the liar than from the credible source.
findings.source: LLM-Test docs/proposals/04_SELF_REGULATION.md section 2 row 23 and section 1 item 8; read this session
findings.numbers: liar amplified at 4 of 5 seeds: drawn false 0.179 / 0.197 / 0.110 / 0.216 / 0.221 vs cred 0.125 / 0.135 / 0.161 / 0.132 / 0.123 (not at s2); untagged default-trust gauge did not fire
findings.implication: AGAINST the belief for structured unreliability. A self-regulated learner attracted by 'learnable' novelty is exploited by liars, like the noisy-TV problem. Unreliable sources need attribution and trust gating, not exposure alone.

findings.claim: Gato serialises data from 604 tasks with different modalities, observations and action spaces into one flat token sequence. The same network with the same weights plays Atari, captions images, chats and stacks blocks with a real robot.
findings.source: Reed et al. 2022, 'A Generalist Agent', arXiv:2205.06175; abstract via search
findings.numbers: 604 tasks; about 1.2B parameters
findings.implication: A shared token stream is the simplest door-opener for A: new modalities are new token types, not new architectures.

findings.claim: Perceiver IO handles arbitrary structured inputs and outputs with cost linear in their size. It produces outputs by querying a latent array and needs no task-specific architecture. It matches a BERT baseline on GLUE without tokenisation.
findings.source: Jaegle et al. 2021/2022, 'Perceiver IO', arXiv:2107.14795 (ICLR 2022); abstract via search
findings.numbers: linear scaling; GLUE parity with BERT without tokenisation; SOTA on Sintel optical flow
findings.implication: A modality-agnostic encoder and decoder keep input and output doors open without committing to discrete tokens.

findings.claim: Unified-IO 2 is the first autoregressive model that both understands and generates images, text, audio and action. It tokenises all of them into a shared semantic space for one encoder-decoder, and needed architectural stabilisers to train.
findings.source: Lu et al. 2023, 'Unified-IO 2', arXiv:2312.17172 (CVPR 2024); abstract via search
findings.numbers: SOTA on GRIT; strong on >35 benchmarks; fine-tuned on 120 datasets; stabilisers 2D RoPE, QK-norm, dynamic packing
findings.implication: A shared stream across four modality families is feasible, but mixed-modal training needs stability engineering. Budget for it in A.

findings.claim: Chameleon is an early-fusion, token-based, mixed-modal family. It needed a training approach that is stable from the start and a parameterisation tailored to that setting.
findings.source: Chameleon Team 2024, arXiv:2405.09818; abstract wording via search. QK-norm details from secondary reviews
findings.numbers: secondary: without QK-norm, training diverged from gradient spikes; the 34B model also needed normalisation reordering and z-loss
findings.implication: Early fusion keeps doors open, but instability is the cost. The stability levers must exist before modalities are mixed at scale.

findings.claim: Transfusion trains one transformer with next-token loss on text and diffusion on images. It scales significantly better than quantising images to discrete tokens, and modality-specific encode and decode layers help further.
findings.source: Zhou et al. 2024, arXiv:2408.11039 (Meta); abstract via search
findings.numbers: up to 7B; images compressible to 16 patches
findings.implication: A discrete-only media path can cap quality. Keep a continuous-input lever beside the discrete one. This bears on 03's codec rows.

findings.claim: Emu3 trains one transformer from scratch with next-token prediction only, over images, text and video tokenised into a discrete space. It outperforms task-specific flagships such as SDXL and LLaVA-1.6 and can generate video.
findings.source: Emu3 Team (BAAI) 2024, arXiv:2409.18869; abstract via search
findings.numbers: qualitative (abstract)
findings.implication: This contradicts Transfusion on discrete tokens. Both routes are live at scale, so the choice stays a lever decided by measurement, not a fixed architectural commitment.

findings.claim: Mixed-modal scaling laws add a synergy-or-competition term per pair of modalities. Competition between modalities is linked to training instability, and training alternates between modalities in an emergent, coordinate-ascent-like way.
findings.source: Aghajanyan et al. 2023, 'Scaling Laws for Generative Mixed-Modal Language Models', arXiv:2301.03728 (ICML 2023); abstract via search
findings.numbers: over 250 experiments; 7 modalities; 8M to 30B parameters; 5-100B tokens
findings.implication: Small models see competition, large ones synergy. A toy-scale finding that adding a modality interferes does not rule a modality out for A.

findings.claim: Early and late fusion reach similar loss at equal compute, and early fusion is better at small parameter counts and easier to deploy. MoE lets models learn modality-specific weights and helps performance significantly.
findings.source: Shukor et al. 2025, 'Scaling Laws for Native Multimodal Models', arXiv:2504.07951 (ICCV 2025 oral); abstract via search
findings.numbers: 457 trained models
findings.implication: A shared stream (early fusion) with modality-aware sparse capacity is the evidence-backed default for a universal-capable core. That is the tree's path: area-based modality addition with FAB groups.

findings.claim: MoMa splits experts into modality-specific groups with learned routing inside each group, and saves large amounts of pretraining compute over a dense early-fusion model.
findings.source: Lin et al. 2024, 'MoMa', arXiv:2407.21770; abstract via search
